title: Which Valley of the Kings Tombs to Visit (and Are Extra Tickets Worth It)?
excerpt: Which Valley of the Kings tombs to visit: Ramesses III, IV and IX on the standard ticket, and whether the Ramesses VI, Tutankhamun and Seti I extras are worth it.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

Quick answer

Your Valley of the Kings ticket covers any three tombs from the day's open list. It costs EGP 750 for a foreign adult (about €12.50) and EGP 375 for a student, as of November 2026. On the standard ticket, take Ramesses III, Ramesses IV and Ramesses IX, all of which are on the current open list. If you buy one extra ticket, buy Ramesses V and VI (KV9, EGP 220, about €3.70): it is the best value in the valley. Tutankhamun (KV62, EGP 700, about €12) is worth it for the story, and Seti I (KV17, EGP 2,000, about €33) only for travellers who come for the art. Nefertari's tomb is not in this valley: it is in the Valley of the Queens, and it has been closed since March 2024. On Sawa's Grand West Bank day, from €60 per person, as listed in November 2026, three tombs on the standard ticket are part of the day and your guide checks the open list at the gate; the extra-ticket tombs are not included.

UNESCO documents the temples and necropolis of ancient Thebes, including Luxor and its West Bank.

The question arrives at the ticket window, not in your hotel room: which three tombs do you want? Most travellers don't know that the ticket covers only three tombs, that the most famous ones cost extra, or that the paint overhead is three thousand years old and still blue. This guide explains how the ticket and the rotation work, ranks the three tombs to pick on the standard ticket, and answers whether Tutankhamun, Seti I and Ramesses VI are worth their extra tickets. It is written by the team behind Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), founded by an Egyptologist guide who has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

What is open in November 2026?

Ten tombs are on the standard list, and four more are open on extra tickets. A guide updated on 3 November 2026 lists these as open on the standard ticket: Ramesses VII (KV1), Ramesses IV (KV2), Ramesses IX (KV6), Merenptah (KV8), Ramesses III (KV11), Tausert and Setnakht (KV14), Seti II (KV15), Ramesses I (KV16), Thutmose IV (KV43) and Siptah (KV47). On extra tickets: Ramesses V and VI (KV9), Seti I (KV17), Tutankhamun (KV62) and, in the West Valley, Ay (WV23). Horemheb (KV57), which older guides recommend, is not on that list.

Tomb rotation is the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities' conservation tool, and the open list changes without ceremony, so treat this as a snapshot. The day's list is posted at the ticket office, and on a guided day your guide checks it at the gate. If you are travelling a few weeks from now, confirm the week you go.

How the ticket actually works

One general ticket admits you to three tombs of your choice from the tombs open that day. More than 60 tombs have been cut into the valley, but only a small number are open at any time. They rotate, closed for conservation and reopened in turn, because humidity from visitors' breath degrades the paint faster than three millennia of sealed darkness did.

The most famous tombs sit outside the three-choice rule and need their own tickets. All of them are bought at the visitor centre only, not inside the valley, so buy everything together before you go through security. A bank card is effectively required at the ticket windows, so carry one, plus some small Egyptian notes for the tram, the toilets and tips.

Prices are as of November 2026 (euros at about EGP 60 to the euro, 8 November 2026). The standard ticket and the Tutankhamun ticket appear on the Ministry's published list, and the other prices agree across several 2026 guides. Egypt revises ticket prices without much notice, so check before you travel.

The ranked list: your three tombs on the standard ticket

  1. Ramesses III (KV11): the best all-rounder. A long, deep tomb with painted side chambers, pillared halls and a mixed programme of funerary texts. It is known for rare scenes of everyday life, including the two blind harpists that give it the nickname "Tomb of the Harpers". It shows you the whole art in one visit and is the safest first pick. Closed? Take Ramesses VII (KV1).
  2. Ramesses IV (KV2): the easiest read. A short, sloping descent straight into decorated chambers, with the king's large granite sarcophagus still in the burial chamber and hundreds of ancient Greek and Coptic graffiti on the walls. It is small, quick and the best tomb for understanding what you will see everywhere else. Closed? Take Tausert and Setnakht (KV14).
  3. Ramesses IX (KV6): the colour. The burial chamber has a vaulted ceiling with the sky goddess Nut and an unusual palette of yellows and deep blues. Ramesses IX died before the tomb was finished, so you can see where the decoration stops, which makes it a good lesson in how a royal tomb was made. Closed? Take Seti II (KV15).

That is the standard ticket done well: one grand tomb, one readable tomb, one colourful tomb. Merenptah (KV8, a steep descent to a giant sarcophagus), Ramesses I (KV16, short and bright) and Siptah (KV47, a long corridor) are good swaps when you want quiet.

Are the extra tickets worth it?

Three tombs sit outside the three-choices rule: Ramesses V and VI (KV9, EGP 220), Tutankhamun (KV62, EGP 700) and Seti I (KV17, EGP 2,000). Here is who should buy each.

Ramesses V and VI (KV9): the extra ticket most travellers should buy

KV9 is where your extra money goes furthest, at a price of about €3.70. Ramesses V began it and Ramesses VI finished it, cutting his own name and images over those of his predecessor, so the tomb carries both kings. Over a hundred metres of passage are decorated. The ceiling of the burial chamber shows the sky goddess Nut twice, once as day and once as night, and the walls carry the Book of Caverns and the Book of the Earth. Nearly a thousand ancient graffiti, in Greek, Latin and Coptic, cover its walls. If you buy one extra ticket, buy this one.

Tutankhamun (KV62): worth it for the story

KV62 is worth the extra ticket if Tutankhamun is part of why you came to Egypt. Howard Carter's team found the top of its sealed steps on 4 November 1922. On 26 November, looking through a small hole in the doorway and asked by Lord Carnarvon what he could see, Carter answered: "Yes, wonderful things." It took ten years to empty the tomb of more than 5,000 objects, which are now displayed at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza.

What the tomb gives you today is the one thing that never left: Tutankhamun himself, in a climate-controlled glass case in the burial chamber, beside his stone sarcophagus. The burial chamber is the only decorated room. The tomb is small, the visit is short, and photography is not allowed. If the Grand Egyptian Museum is already in your plans and your budget is tight, KV9 gives you more decoration for under a third of the price. If the story is why you came, ten minutes at the source of the world's most famous archaeology is worth it.

Seti I (KV17): for travellers who come for the art

The most expensive ticket in the valley and the deepest experience. KV17 is one of the longest and most completely decorated royal tombs, with seventeen chambers and side rooms, nearly all of them in finely carved raised relief with painted detail that the valley never matched again. It is listed as open on its special ticket in 2026, but it has been closed for long periods before, so confirm the week you travel.

Giovanni Belzoni broke into it on 16 October 1817 and found the alabaster sarcophagus, carved inside and out, and no king: Seti I's mummy had been moved to a hiding place at Deir el-Bahari in antiquity. The British Museum decided the price was too high, and the architect Sir John Soane bought the sarcophagus in 1824 for £2,000. It is still the centrepiece of Sir John Soane's Museum in London. If wall art is why you travel, EGP 2,000 is the price of the best version of it in Egypt. If it isn't, KV9 at about a ninth of the price delivers most of the joy.

Not here: Nefertari's tomb and the Valley of the Queens

Nefertari's tomb (QV66) is in the Valley of the Queens, a separate site on the West Bank, not in the Valley of the Kings. Entry to the Valley of the Queens is EGP 220 (about €3.70) and does not include QV66. Nefertari's tomb has been closed for restoration since March 2024, with no reopening date confirmed, as of November 2026. Older pages still quote a price of EGP 2,000 to 2,500 and describe ten-minute visits, but you should not build a day around the tomb until the ticket office confirms it is open. The open tombs of the Valley of the Queens are covered by the Queens' valley ticket, and Seti I is the nearest thing to Nefertari's quality of painting in the Valley of the Kings.

The quiet West Valley: Ay and Amenhotep III

A second cluster of tombs lies a few kilometres away in the West Valley, and almost nobody goes there. The tomb of Ay (WV23), Tutankhamun's successor, is open on a separate EGP 200 ticket (about €3.30) bought at the main office. You need a car or a tour to reach it, and you should allow an extra hour or so. One November 2026 guide also notes that the tomb of Amenhotep III (WV22) reopened in October 2025 after restoration, with limited access: it is not part of the standard ticket, so ask on the day.

What it all costs, and when the Luxor Pass helps

A three-tomb morning costs EGP 750 (about €12.50). The classic version, three tombs plus Ramesses VI plus Tutankhamun, comes to EGP 1,670 (about €28). Adding Seti I brings it to EGP 3,670 (about €61), and adding Ay as well to EGP 3,870 (about €65). Tram fares are extra.

The one thing that changes this arithmetic is the Luxor Pass, which covers many sites on both banks over five days. As reported by Explore Luxor (updated 1 September 2026), the standard pass costs US$130 (or €120) and excludes Seti I and Nefertari, while the premium pass costs US$250 (or €220) and adds both. It is sold in person at Karnak and at the Valley of the Kings visitor centre, in cash dollars or euros. With Nefertari closed, the premium pass's main extra is Seti I, a ticket of about €33, so the pass pays only if you are visiting many sites over several days. Whether either tier covers Tutankhamun and Ramesses VI is unclear, so confirm before you buy, and do the sum against the tickets you will actually use. On a one- or two-day visit, the individual tickets are usually cheaper.

Reading the walls in one lesson

Every royal tomb here is a map of one journey: the sun god Ra's passage through the twelve hours of the night, from sunset to rebirth at dawn. The passage slopes downhill because you descend into the underworld with him. Know three things and every tomb becomes readable:

  • Ra's boat. The Amduat follows it hour by hour through the night.
  • Gates and caverns. The Book of Gates divides the night into twelve guarded gates, and the Book of Caverns shows judgement and punishment below the earth.
  • Nut on the ceiling. The sky goddess swallows the sun at dusk and gives birth to it at dawn.

Near many entrances, the Litany of Ra lists the sun god's 75 forms. And remember why the tombs rotate: your breath is more dangerous to this paint than three thousand years were.

Your morning in the valley, step by step

  1. Go at opening. The gates open at 06:00 and the first hour belongs to early risers, with the air still cool. Buy all your tickets together at the visitor centre, then take the tram.
  2. First: your extra-ticket tomb. KV9 or KV62 before the tour groups arrive. The premium tombs have the smallest chambers and crowd fastest.
  3. Then: the ranked three. Do the deepest tomb last, because heat builds at the far ends by mid-morning, and carry water: there is almost no shade in the valley.
  4. Photography: check at the gate. Personal photos without flash are free in the open tombs. Tripods and professional equipment may fall under separate rules, and the rules for Seti I are not confirmed, so ask.
  5. Out before the heat. Leave for Hatshepsut's temple or Deir el-Medina.

A few habits save money and mood. Decide your three tombs the night before, with one swap ready in case something is closed: nobody chooses well at the window with a queue behind them. Ask your guide to brief you at the entrance, because the corridors are narrow and guards move groups along every few minutes. A guard who steps aside to show you a detail will expect a small tip, so keep low-denomination notes.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Assuming Ramesses VI is included in the standard ticket. It is not: KV9 needs its own EGP 220 ticket.
  • Buying a "Valley of the Kings" ticket and expecting Nefertari. She is in the Valley of the Queens, on a separate ticket, and her tomb is closed.
  • Deciding your three tombs at the gate, in the sun, with a queue behind you.
  • Trying to see six tombs on a summer afternoon. Three tombs plus one extra is a full visit in heat.
  • Buying Seti I before checking whether it is open that week.

Who it suits, and who should skip it

The valley suits almost every traveller: first-timers, solo travellers joining a shared departure, couples, and families with children old enough for steps and heat. It is harder for travellers with limited mobility, because most tombs involve steps, ramps and low light, with KV2 the gentlest. And if you only care about Tutankhamun's treasures, those are at the Grand Egyptian Museum, not here: two hours in the valley is still worth it, but the museum is where your money should go.

The way to cover it all in one day

The Grand West Bank: Tombs, Temples and Deir el-Medina day (about 9 hours, from €60 per person, as listed in November 2026) puts the whole West Bank in one sequence, with hotel pickup in Luxor: the Valley of the Kings with three tombs on the standard ticket, then the Valley of the Queens, the Colossi of Memnon, Hatshepsut's temple, lunch, Medinet Habu and the workers' village of Deir el-Medina. A licensed guide leads the day, and transport, lunch and entrance tickets are included. The special tombs, such as Tutankhamun's and Seti I's, are not included; buy them at the visitor centre if you want them. Nefertari's tomb is closed, so it cannot be part of the visit.

The short version

Three tombs is a menu, not a limit. On the standard ticket take Ramesses III, Ramesses IV and Ramesses IX. Add Ramesses VI (EGP 220, the best value in the valley), then Tutankhamun (EGP 700, the story) and Seti I (EGP 2,000, the art) in that order of appetite, and remember that your breath is harder on the paint than three thousand years were. faq.q: Which tombs should I visit in the Valley of the Kings?
faq.a: On the standard three-tomb ticket: Ramesses III (KV11) for the full art, Ramesses IV (KV2) for the clearest read, and Ramesses IX (KV6) for the colour. All three are on the open list as of November 2026. Add Ramesses V and VI (KV9) as your one extra, at EGP 220 for more than a hundred metres of painted passage, and Tutankhamun (EGP 700) if the story is why you came.

faq.q: Is Tutankhamun's tomb worth the extra ticket?
faq.a: For most first-time visitors, yes, once. It is small and the visit is short, but Tutankhamun himself still lies in the burial chamber Carter opened in 1922, and the Grand Egyptian Museum now displays the treasures taken out of it. Skip it only if you have no attachment to the story and would rather spend the EGP 700 elsewhere.

faq.q: Is Seti I's tomb worth EGP 2,000?
faq.a: If you travel for the art, yes: KV17 is among the most completely decorated tombs in the valley, in finely carved raised relief. If your interest is general, KV9 at EGP 220 delivers much of the wonder for a ninth of the price. Check that KV17 is open the week you travel.

faq.q: Which Valley of the Kings tombs are open right now?
faq.a: Ten tombs are on the standard list as of 3 November 2026 (KV1, KV2, KV6, KV8, KV11, KV14, KV15, KV16, KV43 and KV47), plus KV9, KV17, KV62 and WV23 on extra tickets. The list rotates for conservation, so confirm the week you travel. On a guided day, your guide checks the list at the gate and adjusts the picks.

No. It has been closed for restoration since March 2024, with no reopening date confirmed as of November 2026. It is in the Valley of the Queens, not the Valley of the Kings, so it needs a separate valley ticket and its own ticket if it reopens.

faq.q: Can I take photos inside the tombs?
faq.a: Personal photos are free at Egyptian sites, without flash, which is banned throughout. Reports say no photography is allowed in Tutankhamun's tomb. Ask at the gate about Seti I, tripods and professional equipment.

faq.q: Are the tombs suitable for travellers with limited mobility?
faq.a: Partly. A tram runs from the visitor centre to the valley, and KV2 has the gentlest slope of the big tombs, but most tombs involve steps, ramps and low light. Travellers who cannot manage steps can still see the valley itself and talk through the choices with a guide beforehand.
